terms.definition: A group of changes that must happen all-or-nothing: either all commit or none do.
One partition of the data, on its own machine; a distributed transaction spans several.
Commit makes a transaction's changes permanent; roll back discards them.

before.note: Read Consensus and Sharding first: a distributed transaction coordinates changes across shards and relies on consensus to record its decision durably. The terms below are enough to begin.

stages.name: Basics
body: A single database hands you atomic transactions: begin, change several rows, commit, and either all the changes stick or none do. Once the data is sharded across machines, or split across services that each own a database, that guarantee disappears. A distributed transaction restores all-or-nothing across machines, so a transfer that debits one shard and credits another never leaves money debited but not credited.

There are two broad ways to get it. The strict way is a coordination protocol, classically two-phase commit, that makes every participant agree before anything becomes final. The looser way is the Saga pattern, which Microsoft describes as maintaining data consistency in distributed systems by coordinating a sequence of local transactions across multiple services, with compensating transactions to undo completed steps if a step fails [[ms-saga]]. The strict way keeps strong isolation but holds locks; the saga gives that up for resilience.

Modern distributed databases offer the strict guarantee directly. CockroachDB, for example, bundles multiple SQL statements into a single all-or-nothing transaction with ACID semantics spanning arbitrary tables and rows, even when the data is distributed [[crdb-txns]]. Understanding what that costs, and when a saga is the better trade, is the point of this topic.

terms.definition: A transaction whose changes span multiple shards or services, committed all-or-nothing.
The all-or-nothing property: either every part of the transaction commits or none does.
A protocol that gets every participant to agree before any change becomes final.
A sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action if a later step fails.

stages.name: How it works
body: Two-phase commit uses a coordinator and participants. In the prepare phase the coordinator asks every participant to make its change durable and vote; in the commit phase, if all voted yes, the coordinator durably records "commit" and tells everyone to finalise, otherwise it records "abort" and everyone rolls back. The single most important moment is the commit point: the instant the decision is recorded, after which the outcome is fixed even across crashes.

That recorded decision has to survive failures, which is why distributed transactions sit on consensus: each participant's prepared state and the coordinator's decision are replicated so a crash cannot lose them. CockroachDB's page says that by default, while a transaction is pending, it is isolated from other concurrent transactions with SERIALIZABLE isolation, and that if any part of a transaction fails the whole transaction is aborted and the database is left unchanged [[crdb-txns]].

A saga works differently: there is no global prepare. Each step commits locally and, if a later step fails, the saga runs compensating transactions to reverse the earlier ones. Microsoft notes that a saga has a pivot transaction, the point of no return after which steps only retry forward rather than compensate back [[ms-saga]]. So 2PC decides once and finalises; a saga commits as it goes and undoes on failure.

terms.definition: The component that drives two-phase commit and records the decision.
Each participant makes its change durable and votes yes or no, but nothing is visible yet.
The instant the coordinator durably records the decision; the outcome is then final.
In a saga, the step after which the workflow can only go forward, not compensate back.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: A subtlety of two-phase commit is that participants hold their prepared changes locked from the prepare phase until they hear the decision. If the coordinator is slow or crashes, those locks are held longer, blocking other work on the same data, which is why long or wide 2PC transactions hurt throughput. CockroachDB's page shows the same kind of cost under strict isolation: writes in a SERIALIZABLE transaction can block reads in concurrent SERIALIZABLE transactions [[crdb-txns]].

A saga avoids held locks by committing each step immediately, but it pays a different price: every step needs a correct compensating transaction. Microsoft's page lists irreversible local database changes, because data cannot be rolled back once a participant commits, along with the need to handle transient failures and idempotence, and the limits of compensating transactions. It describes retryable transactions after the pivot as idempotent so the saga can reach its final state [[ms-saga]]. Designing those compensations is the real work of a saga.

The hardest truth is that some operations cannot be perfectly undone. You can refund a charge, but you cannot un-send an email. Spanner's page says serializable isolation is its default and gives the strictest concurrency-control guarantee, external consistency, and it describes write skew as an anomaly that repeatable read isolation can allow [[spanner-txns]]. The choice between 2PC and a saga is really a choice about whether you can afford strict isolation and held locks, or whether you must stay lock-free and design careful compensations instead.

terms.definition: A prepared participant keeps its data locked until the commit decision, blocking other work.
An action that semantically undoes a committed saga step, such as a refund for a charge.
Safe to run more than once with the same effect, required for saga steps and compensations.
The strongest isolation: transactions behave as if run one at a time, hiding concurrency anomalies.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: In practice, pick by the shape of the work. If the data lives in one distributed database that offers ACID transactions, use them: CockroachDB bundles the statements into one all-or-nothing transaction even across distributed data, and by default isolates it with SERIALIZABLE isolation [[crdb-txns]]. If the work spans independent services that each own a database, a saga is the pattern Microsoft recommends when you need consistency without tight coupling and a way to compensate if one operation in the sequence fails [[ms-saga]].

Watch the costs each side hides. Two-phase commit's cost is latency and locking: every participant waits for the decision, and its data is locked until then, so wide or slow transactions reduce concurrency. The topic's CockroachDB post shows one answer, pipelining the consensus rounds so the latency drops without weakening the guarantee. A saga's cost is design effort and exposure: you must write and test a compensation for every step and accept that other readers may briefly see an in-progress workflow.

The strongest practical guidance is to keep distributed transactions rare and small. Model data so that most transactions stay within a single shard or service, where a local transaction suffices; reserve 2PC or sagas for the genuinely cross-boundary cases. Spanner's page points the same way on locking: using secondary indexes to limit the rows a read scans means Spanner locks fewer rows, and the smaller, independent transactions used for partitioned DML hold locks for less time [[spanner-txns]].

terms.definition: A transaction whose data all lives on one shard, so a local transaction suffices and is cheap.
A saga driven by a central orchestrator, versus steps that trigger each other through events.
The time to coordinate and commit, dominated by participant round trips in 2PC.
How much other work a transaction blocks; smaller, shard-local transactions keep it low.

misconceptions.myth: You can just write to each shard in turn and it will be fine.
misconceptions.truth: A crash between writes leaves a partial result. CockroachDB's page describes the all-or-nothing alternative: if any part of a transaction fails, the entire transaction is aborted and the database is left unchanged [[crdb-txns]].

misconceptions.myth: Two-phase commit is free once all participants vote yes.
misconceptions.truth: Participants hold locks from prepare until the decision, so wide or slow 2PC transactions block other work.

misconceptions.myth: A saga is simpler because it has no coordinator.
misconceptions.truth: A saga needs a compensation for every step, and Microsoft's page notes that local database changes are irreversible once committed and that pivot and retryable steps cannot be compensated [[ms-saga]].

misconceptions.myth: Strong distributed transactions mean you never think about transaction cost.
misconceptions.truth: Spanner's page describes locks that read-write transactions might acquire and ways to lock fewer rows, so even strong transactions have a locking cost to manage [[spanner-txns]].
